title: A church needing reform
hook: voices across the church agreed it needed reform; the sale of indulgences became the spark
tomorrow: The righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17)

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the middle centuries, treasure in earthen vessels: cathedrals and crusades, saints and scandals. Your line was both are true. Where did you find the other half of a story? Day eight hundred fifty-one.

A procession comes into a German town square. Banners, candles, a cross, and in the middle, carried with great ceremony, a papal document. A preacher climbs up and begins. Give toward the building of a great church in Rome, he says, and receive a letter of indulgence. For yourself. Even for your mother and father, who have died. People push forward with coins. And a little rhyme starts going around, one that tradition puts in the mouth of a preacher named Tetzel: as soon as the coin in the box rings, a soul out of purgatory springs. A new block begins with today's word.

First, what an indulgence is, in Catholic teaching, because the word is easy to mock and harder to explain. When a sin is confessed and forgiven, Catholics say, its guilt is taken away, but some of its damage can remain, a kind of debt that still needs healing, in this life or in purgatory. An indulgence is the church releasing some of that debt, drawing on the goodness of Christ and the saints, for someone who prays, makes a pilgrimage or does a good work. Giving to the poor or to a church could be one of those works. You can see where it went wrong. A gift became a price. Preachers sold letters from town to town, some promising far more than the church taught, and the money ran to building projects and to people's pockets. The Bible already had a word for buying holy things. In Acts, a man named Simon offers the apostles money for the power of the Spirit, and Peter answers, in the King James Bible: "Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money." Something else belongs in this story. People inside the church were already saying it needed reform: preachers, scholars like Erasmus, bishops, councils, ordinary believers. Catholics would later forbid the selling of indulgences outright, while still teaching what indulgences are. Reformed Protestants later had a saying for the idea in today's line, that the church must always be reformed. And a much later Catholic council, the Second Vatican Council, spoke of the church as always in need of being purified. The disagreement that comes next is real. But the hunger for reform was not only Protestant.

Here's the practice: name one thing in you that needs reform. Not your whole life. One thing. A habit that has slowly turned from a gift into a price. Something you started doing for good reasons that now runs on autopilot, or on fear, or on money. Settle, and breathe. Let it come to mind. Don't punish yourself for it. Just name it plainly, the way you'd name a crack in a wall you mean to fix. If you pray, you can hold it before God. If you don't, hold it in the light for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Indulgence. In Catholic teaching, the church's release from some of the debt that remains after a sin is forgiven. Its sale became the spark for the reformations.
Your line: always reforming. Today, take the one thing you named and change one small part of it, once, before the day ends. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church still teaches about indulgences and grants them for prayer, pilgrimage and works of charity, never for sale; Protestant churches do not use indulgences, and some Reformed churches use the saying 'always reforming' about themselves.

fork.setup: you're in the town square. the preacher says a coin will buy a letter of indulgence for your mother, who died last winter. what do you do?
options: go and ask your priest what it really means.
fork.reveal: people paid, for themselves and for their dead. soon a monk who heard their confessions began asking hard questions about it.

trapdoor: what you thought: paying the church to sin.
what it means: in Catholic teaching, a release from the debt left after a sin is forgiven, which in this era was being sold.
what a scholar hears: Peter's word to Simon in Acts, and a call for reform that came from across the church, Catholic as well as Protestant.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'by 1500, many Catholics agreed' is cut; no dates or counts are stated. The hook field is reworded ('voices across the church agreed').

Catholic teaching on indulgences (guilt forgiven, temporal punishment remaining, the treasury of merits) is paraphrased from the Catechism 1471–1479; a Catholic scholar should confirm the plain-language wording ('a kind of debt that still needs healing').

The Tetzel rhyme is attributed to tradition; it is usually quoted in German as 'Wenn das Geld im Kasten klingt, die Seele aus dem Fegefeuer springt'. The building fund was for St. Peter's Basilica; 'a great church in Rome' is left general.
'Catholics would later forbid the selling of indulgences outright': the Council of Trent (1562) abolished indulgence-sellers (quaestores); no date stated. Confirm.

'Always reforming' (ecclesia semper reformanda) is attributed to later Reformed Protestants; the Catholic parallel is Lumen Gentium 8 ('semper purificanda') and Unitatis Redintegratio 6. 'In the last century' refers to Vatican II; confirm the phrasing.
Fork: answer is what people did historically (they bought letters); framed as history, not a moral test.
Fairness check: the teach explains the Catholic doctrine before the abuse, and says the hunger for reform was not only Protestant.

Editor pass: 'door to door' (inaccurate picture) changed to 'from town to town'; stock line 'here's the part that often gets left out' cut; sweeping 'the church was full of people' and 'belonged to everyone' softened.
Second editor: 'a Catholic council in the last century' (a date claim the cited text does not make) changed to name the Second Vatican Council without a date.
Auditor (day 847-856 pass): checked; Acts 8:20 matches the KJV; Catholic doctrine given before the abuse, and reform voices shown on all sides. No change.
